subject: Economics
name: Economics, Year 12: Australia's economy
about: HSC, Australia's place, economic issues and policies
syllabus: NSW Economics Stage 6 Syllabus (2009), HSC (Year 12) course, Topics 2 to 4

units.title: Australia's place in the global economy

points.title: What Australia exports and imports
points.brief: Australia's exports are led by resources such as iron ore, coal and gas, plus education, tourism and farm goods. It imports mostly manufactured goods and fuel.

points.title: Australia's trading partners
points.brief: Australia's trade has shifted from Britain and Europe towards Asia. China is its largest trading partner, followed by Japan, South Korea and the United States.

points.title: The terms of trade
points.brief: The terms of trade compare export prices with import prices. When commodity prices rise, Australia's terms of trade improve and national income rises.

points.title: Foreign investment in Australia
points.brief: Foreign direct investment buys a lasting stake in Australian businesses. Portfolio investment buys shares and bonds. Both fund investment that domestic saving cannot.

points.title: The capital and financial account
points.brief: Records flows of investment and lending into and out of Australia. A current account deficit is matched by a surplus here.

points.title: Why Australia runs current account deficits
points.brief: Australia has long invested more than it saves, borrowing the difference from abroad, and pays large income flows to foreign investors.

points.title: Foreign debt and foreign equity
points.brief: Borrowing from abroad builds net foreign debt, and selling assets to foreigners builds foreign equity. Together they make net foreign liabilities.

points.title: Sustainability of the current account
points.brief: A deficit is less of a worry if it funds productive investment and export growth. The debt servicing ratio shows how much export income goes to paying interest.

points.title: How the Australian dollar is set
points.brief: The Australian dollar floats, so its value is set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market.

points.title: What moves the Australian dollar
points.brief: Commodity prices, interest rate differences with other countries, investor confidence and speculation all move the dollar.

points.title: Appreciation and depreciation
points.brief: A rising dollar makes imports cheaper and exports dearer. A falling dollar helps exporters but raises import prices and inflation.

points.title: The trade-weighted index
points.brief: The TWI measures the Australian dollar against a basket of trading partners' currencies, weighted by how much trade we do with each.

points.title: Floating and fixed exchange rates
points.brief: Australia floated its dollar in 1983. A floating rate adjusts on its own and cushions shocks, while a fixed rate needs the central bank to defend it.

chapters.title: Trade policy and globalisation in Australia

points.title: Trade liberalisation in Australia
points.brief: Since the 1980s Australia has cut tariffs sharply, exposing industries to competition and shifting resources to more efficient uses.

points.title: Australia's free trade agreements
points.brief: Australia has trade agreements with partners such as China, Japan, Korea and the United States, and regional ones such as RCEP and the CPTPP.

points.title: Effects of globalisation on Australia
points.brief: Globalisation has brought cheaper imports, foreign investment and access to markets, along with job losses in some industries and exposure to global shocks.

points.title: The resources boom
points.brief: Rising demand from China in the 2000s lifted commodity prices and mining investment, raising national income and the dollar but squeezing other export industries.

points.title: Aggregate supply and productivity
points.brief: Growth over the long term depends on more and better inputs, especially productivity, the output per hour of work.

points.title: The business cycle
points.brief: Real GDP rises and falls around its long-term trend through upswings, booms, downswings and recessions.

points.title: Measuring unemployment in Australia
points.brief: The ABS Labour Force Survey counts someone as unemployed if they had no paid work in the survey week, looked for work and could start.

points.title: The natural rate of unemployment
points.brief: The rate below which unemployment cannot fall without inflation rising, made of frictional, seasonal and structural unemployment. Estimates for Australia change over time.

points.title: Hidden and long-term unemployment
points.brief: Hidden unemployment is people who want work but have stopped looking. Long-term unemployment means being out of work for a year or more, which erodes skills.

points.title: Underemployment
points.brief: People who have work but want more hours. Australia's underemployment rate is often close to or above its unemployment rate.

points.title: Headline and underlying inflation
points.brief: Headline inflation is the change in the whole CPI. Underlying measures, such as the trimmed mean, remove the biggest price swings to show the trend.

points.title: Inflationary expectations
points.brief: If people expect prices to rise, they ask for higher wages and firms raise prices, so expectations can make inflation keep going.

points.title: What external stability means
points.brief: An economy is externally stable when its current account deficit and foreign liabilities can be sustained and its currency is not prone to sharp swings.

points.title: Vulnerability to the terms of trade
points.brief: Australia's dependence on commodity exports makes national income, the dollar and government revenue rise and fall with world commodity prices.

points.title: Credit ratings and foreign confidence
points.brief: Agencies rate how likely a government is to repay its debt. A lower rating can raise borrowing costs and weaken the dollar.

points.title: Sources of income and wealth
points.brief: Income comes from wages, profits, interest, rent and welfare. Wealth is assets, such as housing, shares and superannuation, less debts.

points.title: The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient
points.brief: The Lorenz curve plots the share of income held by each share of households. The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (equal) to 1 (one person holds everything).

points.title: Inequality in Australia
points.brief: Wealth is much less evenly spread than income in Australia, and differences exist by age, gender, location and for First Nations Australians.

points.title: Costs and benefits of inequality
points.brief: Some inequality rewards effort and risk. Large gaps can harm health, social cohesion and growth, and waste the skills of people left behind.

points.title: Ecologically sustainable development
points.brief: Growth that meets today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

points.title: The environment as a market failure
points.brief: Pollution is an external cost markets ignore, and clean air and a stable climate are public goods, so markets overuse the environment.

points.title: Climate change and the economy
points.brief: Rising emissions bring higher temperatures, more extreme weather and costs to farming, health and infrastructure.

points.title: Environmental policies in Australia
points.brief: Australia uses regulation, emissions limits on large emitters, support for renewable energy and market-based tools to cut emissions.

points.title: Macroeconomic and microeconomic policy
points.brief: Macroeconomic policy, fiscal and monetary, manages demand in the short run. Microeconomic policy lifts the economy's capacity over the long run.

points.title: Budget outcomes
points.brief: A budget is in deficit when spending exceeds revenue and in surplus when revenue exceeds spending. The change in the outcome shows whether policy is expansionary or contractionary.

points.title: Automatic stabilisers
points.brief: In a downturn, tax revenue falls and welfare spending rises on their own, cushioning the economy without any new decision.

points.title: Structural and cyclical budget parts
points.brief: The cyclical part of the budget moves with the business cycle. The structural part reflects the government's policy choices.

points.title: Government debt
points.brief: Deficits are funded by selling government bonds, which builds public debt. Interest on the debt is a cost to future budgets.

points.title: The RBA and the cash rate
points.brief: The RBA's Monetary Policy Board sets a target for the cash rate, the interest rate banks pay each other on overnight loans, and steers it through its market operations.

points.title: The inflation target
points.brief: The RBA aims to keep inflation between 2 and 3% on average, alongside full employment.

points.title: How monetary policy works
points.brief: A change in the cash rate flows through to loan and deposit rates, the dollar and asset prices, changing spending and inflation over one to two years.

points.title: Unconventional monetary policy
points.brief: When the cash rate was near zero in 2020 and 2021, the RBA bought government bonds and gave banks cheap funding to keep interest rates low.

points.title: Limits of monetary policy
points.brief: Monetary policy works with long and uneven time lags, cannot target one region or industry, and can be weakened by global events.

points.title: Microeconomic reform
points.brief: Policies that make industries and markets more efficient and productive, lifting the economy's long-term capacity.

points.title: Competition policy
points.brief: Laws enforced by the ACCC stop firms from fixing prices or abusing market power, keeping markets competitive.

points.title: Labour market reform
points.brief: Changes to how wages and conditions are set, such as the move to enterprise bargaining, aim to make the labour market more flexible and productive.

points.title: Tax reform
points.brief: Changing the tax system to make it simpler, fairer or better for growth, as when the GST replaced older sales taxes in 2000.

points.title: Costs of microeconomic reform
points.brief: Reform can cost jobs in protected industries, widen inequality and take years to pay off, so it can be hard to win support for.

points.title: Time lags in policy
points.brief: Recognising a problem, deciding on a policy and seeing its effects all take time, so policy can arrive too late or too strongly.

points.title: Global influences on policy
points.brief: In a small open economy like Australia, world events and other countries' policies can outweigh domestic policy.

points.title: Political constraints
points.brief: Governments may avoid unpopular choices, such as cutting spending, especially near an election.

points.title: The policy mix
points.brief: Fiscal, monetary and microeconomic policies work best when they pull the same way and suit the problem the economy faces.
